results.summary: This design computes the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two 4-bit numbers using an optimized Euclidean algorithm. The two numbers are entered via DIP switches, with a num_okey switch controlling register loading, and the result is displayed on a seven-segment display. The implementation separates the control unit and datapath to optimize the algorithm. No external hardware is required beyond the switches and display.

This design blinks the eight output LEDs in various patterns, with a function switch selecting between a simple blinky mode and a double 14-bit counter mode. In counter mode, two output control switches select which bits of the counters are shown, and a pause switch halts counting. The design is intended to work with the mcpi module, likely as an external display or counter. The documentation is minimal, with no explanation of the internal implementation.

This design estimates the value of Pi using the Monte Carlo method, generating random x and y coordinates in 8-bit fixed-point format and checking whether they fall inside a unit circle. Two control switches select what the 8-bit output displays: total sample points, points inside the circle, or a toggle signal for each sample and inside point. An external edge counter is recommended to accumulate the results, with the Funny Blinky design suggested as a possible choice. The design relies on an internal random number generator and provides no further details on its implementation.

This design decodes a 4-bit input value into the seven segment patterns required to display a hexadecimal digit. It includes latch and blank inputs, as well as a decimal point output, and is described as a modern take on the classic TIL311 display driver. The test instructions mention that after reset, a counter should increase by one every second, but the design itself does not include a counter, suggesting the test may be for a different project or an error. No external hardware is specified.

This design is a 4-bit ALU inspired by the Supercon.6 badge, implemented as a finite state machine with combinational logic in Verilog. It takes two 4-bit data inputs and a control signal, and produces a 4-bit result along with a carry-out. The design is tested using cocotb, a Python-based verification framework. No external hardware is required.

This design reads an incremental rotary encoder and displays the resulting count on a seven-segment display. It samples the encoder pins every clock cycle, detects rising edges on pin A, and increments or decrements a 4-bit counter based on the state of pin B, with a debounce period of 125 clock cycles. The design requires an external rotary encoder connected to pins A and B. After reset, turning the encoder updates the displayed count.

This design implements a single fracturable 5-input lookup table (LUT) that can be configured via serial SRAM or FLASH frames. It receives 92-bit LUT configuration frames serially, four bits per cycle, and evaluates the LUT every 23 clock cycles. The last 283 LUT output values are stored on-chip to serve as inputs for subsequent LUTs, and the design includes two FPGA input pins and seven output pins plus a debug pin. Testing is described as tricky, and external serial memory is required for configuration.

This project is titled 'Secret File' and provides no meaningful documentation; the one-line description says 'Nothing to see here' and the how-it-works section states 'Leving it alone works'. The design has a clock input and eight output bits, but no explanation of their function. The test instructions say 'Don't test me' and the external hardware requirement is a shredder, indicating a humorous or intentionally undocumented design. There is insufficient information to determine what the design actually does.

This design counts from 0 to 9 on a seven-segment display, incrementing once per second. It uses a register and combinational logic to drive the display segments. After reset, the counter should increase by one every second. No external hardware is required beyond the display.

This design is a 2-bit ALU that performs 16 different operations on two 2-bit inputs, A and B, selected by a 4-bit opcode. The result is an 8-bit output. To use it, provide the A and B inputs, set the opcode for the desired operation, and observe the result on ALU_out. No external hardware is required.
